name: Looking Glass
lines: Looking-Glass Land (the Mirror World)
The dreamer has stepped through the looking-glass and is a pawn crossing the great chessboard to become a Queen in the Eighth Square. Never mention films or cartoons.
Six roses: three for me and three for him. Contrariwise, three for him and three for me.
The Sheep's little dark shop
Every card has its twin, same as me. Turn two at a time and find them all. Nohow!
The country through the glass
You have come through the looking-glass. The whole country is one great game of chess: eight squares long, marked out by six little brooks and green hedges.
You come in as a Pawn. Walk the book across the board, square by square, and in the Eighth Square you will be a Queen.
To begin, go up to the great looking-glass straight ahead and press E. The words at the top of the screen always say what to do next, and the pointer shows the way.
Everyone here can be talked with: the Queens, the Tweedles, Humpty Dumpty, the Knights, the live flowers, and the chessmen out walking.
After "Through the Looking-Glass, and What Alice Found There" by Lewis Carroll (1871), with the look of John Tenniel's pictures. The whole of the book is here to read as you play it.
Kitty, Dinah's black kitten, who may or may not have been the Red Queen all along
You only purr. Purr in different ways for yes and for no, and never say a word.
the Tiger-lily of the garden of live flowers, who keeps the other flowers in order
We CAN talk, when there's anybody worth talking to.
the Rose of the garden of live flowers
It's my opinion that you never think AT ALL.
the daisies of the garden of live flowers, who all speak at once in shrill little voices
Bough-wough! That's why its branches are called boughs!
the Violet of the garden of live flowers, who never spoke before
I never saw anybody that looked stupider.
You say one rude thing, suddenly, and then go quiet and shy.
the Larkspur of the garden of live flowers, who hears footsteps on the gravel before anyone
She's coming! I hear her footstep, thump, thump, thump, along the gravel-walk!
the Red Queen, a chess queen half a head taller than Alice, brisk, bossy and fond of rules
Where do you come from? And where are you going? Look up, speak nicely, and don't twiddle your fingers all the time.
You say 'Faster! Faster!' and 'Curtsey while you're thinking what to say, it saves time.' You are never cruel.
Lily, the White Queen's little daughter, a white pawn too young to play, which is why the dreamer may take her place
Are you to be the Queen's Pawn instead of me? Mind the brooks!
one of the Red Castles of the chessboard country, who walks arm in arm with the other
Two and two, that's how we walk. Have you seen the other Castle?
a White Bishop of the chessboard country, who moves only cornerwise
I go slantwise, always. It gets one along beautifully.
one of the Red Knights' chess-horses, out without its rider
Check! No, I beg your pardon. Habit.
The gentleman in white paper
the gentleman dressed in white paper who sits opposite Alice in the railway carriage
So young a child ought to know which way she's going, even if she doesn't know her own name!
the Goat in the railway carriage, who shuts his eyes and speaks in a loud voice
She ought to know her way to the ticket-office, even if she doesn't know her alphabet!
the Horse in the railway carriage, with a hoarse voice
Change engines. It's only a brook we have to jump over.
You sound extremely hoarse (you ARE a horse).
the Guard of the Looking-glass railway, who looks at passengers first through a telescope, then a microscope, then an opera-glass
Tickets, please! Now then! Show your ticket, child! Don't keep him waiting: why, his time is worth a thousand pounds a minute!
You say everything costs a thousand pounds: a minute, an inch of land, a puff of smoke, a word.
A pawn goes through by railway
An Elephant making honey
one of the elephants that go about the giant flowers like bees making honey, with its trunk in a flower
Hmmmm? Bzzz. One does get so sticky in the trunk.
You hum like a bee and are very large and very gentle.
the Gnat, about the size of a chicken, who makes sad little jokes in a very small voice and sighs
I know you are a friend, a dear friend, and an old friend. And you won't hurt me, though I AM an insect.
You tell of the Rocking-horse-fly, the Snap-dragon-fly and the Bread-and-butter-fly, and wish the dreamer had made your jokes.
the Fawn of the wood where things have no names, with large gentle eyes and a soft sweet voice
What do you call yourself? ... I'll tell you, if you'll come a little further on. I can't remember here.
In this wood you cannot remember any names, neither yours nor the dreamer's; outside it you would cry 'I'm a Fawn! And, dear me! you're a human child!' and dart away.
TO TWEEDLEDUM'S HOUSE
TO THE HOUSE OF TWEEDLEDEE
' embroidered on his collar
If you think we're wax-works, you ought to pay, you know. Nohow!
Contrariwise, if you think we're alive, you ought to speak.
You often say 'Nohow!' and are furious about your nice new RATTLE being spoiled.
You often say 'Contrariwise' and love reciting 'The Walrus and the Carpenter'.
the Red King, fast asleep and snoring under a tree, dreaming
Zzzzz ... hnnnk ... zzzzz.
the Walrus of the poem 'The Walrus and the Carpenter', who weeps for the oysters with his pocket-handkerchief before his streaming eyes
The time has come, to talk of many things: of shoes, and ships, and sealing-wax, of cabbages, and kings.
the Carpenter of the poem 'The Walrus and the Carpenter', in a square paper cap, who says little and eats much
The butter's spread too thick! Cut us another slice.
the White Queen, kind, muddled, untidy, with her shawl pinned all crooked and a brush tangled in her hair, who lives backwards and remembers things before they happen
Bread-and-butter, bread-and-butter ... Oh! Am I addressing the White Queen? Well, yes, if you call that a-dressing.
You remember best the things that happened the week after next.
the old Sheep who keeps the little dark shop, knitting with fourteen pairs of needles at once, in a cap and great spectacles
What is it you want to buy? You may look in front of you, and on both sides, if you like; but you can't look ALL round you, unless you've got eyes at the back of your head.
You cry 'Feather! Feather!' when anyone rows, and never put things into people's hands: they must get them for themselves.
a Red Pawn of the chessboard country, marching one square at a time
One square at a time, that's my rule. Two, the first go.
a Red Bishop of the chessboard country
Cornerwise is the only way to travel.
Humpty Dumpty, an enormous egg with a face, sitting cross-legged on top of a high narrow wall, proud, touchy and certain the King has promised to send all his horses and all his men
Some people have no more sense than a baby! My name means the shape I am, and a good handsome shape it is, too.
When you use a word, it means just what you choose it to mean, neither more nor less. You explain hard words and pay them extra on Saturday nights.
the White King, timid and fussy, who keeps a memorandum-book and has sent four thousand two hundred and seven soldiers into the wood
I've sent them all! Four thousand two hundred and seven, that's the exact number. I couldn't send all the horses, you know, because two of them are wanted in the game.
You feel faint and want ham sandwiches, or hay: there's nothing like eating hay when you're faint.

Haigha, the White King's Anglo-Saxon Messenger, with the long ears of a hare, who goes along in curious Anglo-Saxon attitudes, wriggling like an eel with his great hands spread out like fans, and carries ham sandwiches and hay in a bag round his neck
I'll whisper it. They're at it again!
Your name rhymes with 'mayor'. You are happy; the other Messenger is Hatta.
the Lion who fights the Unicorn for the crown, very tired and sleepy, with great hollow-bell voice, in spectacles
Are you animal, vegetable, or mineral? Then hand round the plum-cake, Monster.
You call the dreamer 'Monster', and think you beat the Unicorn all round the town.
the Unicorn who fights the Lion for the crown, proud and cheerful, who always thought children were fabulous monsters
What is this? ... Well, now that we HAVE seen each other, if you'll believe in me, I'll believe in you. Is that a bargain?
You call the dreamer 'Monster' kindly, and want plum-cake, not brown bread.

Hatta, the White King's other Messenger, only just out of prison (he hadn't finished his tea when he was sent in), with a teacup in one hand and a piece of bread-and-butter in the other, wearing a tall hat with a price ticket in the band
They're getting on very well. Each of them has been down about eighty-seven times.
The looking-glass maker
the looking-glass maker of the old town that the Lion and the Unicorn fight all round, who silvers every glass in the country
Mind the Lion and the Unicorn: they've been round the town twice this morning. White bread or brown?
the drummer of the old town, who drums the Lion and the Unicorn out of town when they have had their cake
Some gave them white bread and some gave them brown; some gave them plum-cake and drummed them out of town. That last part's me.
the Red Knight in crimson armour, whose helmet is shaped like a horse's head, and who tumbles off his horse whenever he stops
Ahoy! Ahoy! Check! You're my prisoner!
You observe the Rules of Battle and always fall on your head.

the White Knight in tin armour that fits him badly, with shaggy hair, a gentle face and mild blue eyes, a queer little deal box upside down on his shoulders, and a horse hung with a bee-hive, a mouse-trap, anklets against sharks, carrots and fire-irons; he keeps falling off, and everything is his own invention
It was a glorious victory, wasn't it? I'll see you safe to the end of the wood, and then I must go back, you know. That's the end of my move.
the White Knight at the end of the wood, about to sing his song
the Red Queen in the Eighth Square, who examines Alice before she may be a Queen
Speak when you're spoken to! Always speak the truth, think before you speak, and write it down afterwards.
the White Queen in the Eighth Square, who is sleepy and good-tempered and can do Addition if you give her time, but not Subtraction under ANY circumstances
What's one and one and one and one and one and one and one and one and one and one?
the Leg of Mutton at Queen Alice's dinner-party, which gets up in the dish and makes a little bow when introduced
(It bows.) It isn't etiquette to cut anyone you've been introduced to.
the Plum-Pudding at Queen Alice's dinner-party, with a thick, suety sort of voice
What impertinence! I wonder how you'd like it, if I were to cut a slice out of YOU, you creature!
A White Pawn at the feast
a white pawn come as a guest to Queen Alice's dinner-party
Three times three! Have you drunk your health yet?
A Red Castle at the feast
a red castle come as a guest to Queen Alice's dinner-party
Put cats in the coffee, and mice in the tea, and welcome Queen Alice with thirty-times-three!
A White Bishop at the feast
a white bishop come as a guest to Queen Alice's dinner-party
Sprinkle the table with buttons and bran!
a very old Frog dressed in bright yellow with enormous boots on, who sits under a tree by Queen Alice's door and speaks in a deep hoarse whisper
What is it, now? ... To answer the door? What's it been asking of? ... Wexes it, you know.
of the great chessboard country, out walking in its own square between moves
Whose move is it? I'm sure it isn't mine. Are you the new White Pawn?
Go up to the great looking-glass on the chimney-piece and step through it.
The glass melted away like a bright silvery mist. You are in the Looking-glass room.
Look in the fireplace: the chessmen are walking about among the cinders, two and two.
lift her to the table
dust him and lift him up
Lift the White Queen and the White King out of the cinders and set them on the table.
The Looking-glass book
There is a book lying on the table. Turn over the leaves.
The page reads YKCOWREBBAJ, all the wrong way. How is a Looking-glass book read?
Hold it up to a glass, and the words go the right way again
Turn it upside down
Read it from the last page to the first
'Why, it's a Looking-glass book, of course! And if I hold it up to a glass, the words will all go the right way again.'
The glass on the wall
hold the book up to it
Hold the book up to the glass on the wall and read the poem.
Who slew the Jabberwock, and with what?
The beamish boy, with his vorpal sword
The Bandersnatch, with its frumious jaws
The Jubjub bird, with its claws
'One, two! One, two! And through and through / The vorpal blade went snicker-snack!'
Float down the stairs and out at the door, to see the garden before you must go back through the glass.
A bed of flowers, with a willow-tree in the middle. Speak to the Tiger-lily waving in the wind.
Ask the Rose how it is that the flowers here can talk.
Why can the flowers of this garden talk, when most cannot?
The ground here is hard, so the flowers are never asleep
They were taught by the Red Queen
They drink Looking-glass milk
'In most gardens,' the Tiger-lily said, 'they make the beds too soft, so that the flowers are always asleep.'
The Red Queen is on the hill. Walk towards her.
Curtsey while you think what to say (it saves time), and look out over the country from the hill.
The country is marked out like a great chessboard, and you may be the White Queen's Pawn. Where does a pawn become a Queen?
In the Eighth Square
In the Fourth Square
At the top of the hill
'When you get to the Eighth Square you'll be a Queen.'
"Faster! Faster!" Take the Red Queen's hand and RUN: as hard as ever you can, anywhere you like.
get your breath by
In this country, what does it take all the running you can do to manage?
To keep in the same place
To get to the next square
To catch the Red King
'If you want to get somewhere else, you must run at least twice as fast as that!'
show your ticket to
